Leonard Woods
len'ərd woodz
n. (Leonard Woods, 1774–1854, first professor of theology at Andover Theological Seminary)
English surname Woods, a dweller by the wood; Leonard, from Germanic, lion-strong.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leonard Woods was the first Abbot Professor of Christian Theology at Andover and taught there for thirty-six years. He had been instrumental in the compromise between the moderate Calvinists and the Old Calvinists that made the seminary possible in 1808, and he drafted the Andover creed which every professor was required to subscribe every five years. His Letters to Unitarians answered Henry Ware and William Ellery Channing on the deity of Christ, the atonement, and human depravity, and his five-volume collected works set out a moderate Calvinism that held imputation, inability, and definite atonement while pressing the free offer of the gospel on all. He opposed the New Haven revisions and he opposed the drift of his own younger colleagues. Tit 1:9 names the duty he discharged for three decades: holding fast the faithful word as he had been taught.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief summary of the articles of Christian faith, and subscription as the act of signing one's name in attestation.

expand to see more

CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a symbol; a formula of belief.

SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation by writing the name.

UNITA'RIAN, n. One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, and ascribes divinity to God the Father only.

Key Scripture

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

2Ti 1:9 — "Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,"

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Heb 10:23 — "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)"

Modern Corruption

He wrote the creed his successors subscribed and then watched them reinterpret it.

expand to see more

The Andover creed is one of the clearest lessons in American church history about confessional subscription. It was tight, it was renewed every five years, and within forty years of Woods's death the faculty was teaching a progressive theology while still signing it, on the ground that the words admitted a broader construction. Heb 10:23 commands us to “hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23), and a profession held with mental reservation is not held.

Woods's controversy with the Unitarians shows the other side of the man. Against Channing he argued the deity of Christ and the real satisfaction of the atonement, and against the New Haven men he argued inability; the two defences come from one principle, that the words of Scripture bind. Gal 1:8 is why he refused to call the Unitarian scheme a variety of Christianity. 2Ti 1:9 grounds the salvation he preached in God's own purpose and grace given before the world began, which is the doctrine the Andover of 1890 no longer taught.

Usage

"“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — thirty-six years of it."

"“hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) — what subscription means."

"“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — why Unitarianism was not a variety."
